title: Template literals and tagged templates
hook: Backtick strings (`...`) are template literals: they support multi-line text, embedded ${expressions}, and tagged templates where a function receives raw string parts plus interpolated values — the modern replacement for C# raw strings and string.Format.

sections.heading: What are template literals and tagged templates?

blocks.text: A **template literal** is a string delimited by backticks `` ` `` instead of quotes. It can span multiple lines without escape sequences and embed expressions via `${expression}`. A **tagged template** calls a function (the tag) with processed string segments and evaluated values: `` tag`Hello ${name}` ``. Tags power libraries like styled-components, GraphQL gql, and HTML sanitization. **String.raw** is a built-in tag that preserves backslashes in raw segments.

entries.plainDefinition: A backtick-delimited string supporting interpolation and multi-line content.
entries.example: `Hello ${user.name}` embeds the name at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Embedding an expression inside a template literal using ${ ... }.
entries.example: `Total: ${price * qty}` — expressions are evaluated and coerced to string.

entries.plainDefinition: A function invoked with (strings, ...values) when placed before a template literal.
entries.example: css`color: ${theme.primary};` — css controls how strings and values combine.

entries.plainDefinition: The frozen raw string segments including escape sequences before processing.
entries.example: String.raw`\n` is backslash-n, not a newline character.

sections.heading: Why template literals replace old string patterns

blocks.text: Concatenating `"Hello " + name + "!"` is error-prone and hard to read. Template literals mirror C# interpolated strings `$"Hello {name}"` and raw strings `"""..."""` for JSON fixtures. Use them for HTML snippets, log lines, SQL parameterization (with tags that enforce escaping), and internationalization placeholders. Never inject unsanitized user input into HTML templates — tagged sanitizers or dedicated APIs are required.

blocks.title: C# raw strings vs backticks
blocks.body: C# 11 raw strings use triple quotes for JSON and CSV. JavaScript backticks already allow multi-line JSON with minimal escaping. C# $"{x}" maps to `${x}` in JavaScript. Neither replaces parameterized queries — always bind parameters.

items.title: Parse static and dynamic parts
items.body: The parser splits the literal into static string segments and ${ expression } holes.

items.title: Evaluate expressions
items.body: Each ${ ... } expression runs left to right; results convert ToString.

items.title: Concatenate (untagged)
items.body: Static parts and stringified values join into one string value.

items.title: Tagged path
items.body: If a tag function precedes the literal, it receives strings (with raw property) and values, returning any type.

sections.heading: Code walkthrough: literals, interpolation, and tags

snippet.label: Multi-line and interpolated strings
snippet.explanation: Newlines are literal inside backticks. ${} accepts any expression. Escape backticks inside with \` if needed.

snippet.label: Nested templates and expression rules
snippet.explanation: Nested templates are legal. Objects coerce via toString or Symbol.toPrimitive. Prefer explicit String(x) in logs.

snippet.label: Tagged template function signature
snippet.explanation: Tag receives frozen strings array (with .raw) and evaluated values separately — enables safe DSL builders.

snippet.label: String.raw built-in tag
snippet.explanation: String.raw reads the raw cooked segments. Useful for regex patterns and Windows paths in tests.

blocks.title: Top pitfalls
blocks.body: Building SQL or HTML with untagged templates and user input — injection risk. Assuming tagged templates always return strings — tags can return objects (styled components). Forgetting that undefined in ${} becomes "undefined" string in output. Using single quotes when you need interpolation — only backticks support ${}. Nested unescaped backticks ending the literal early.

blocks.title: Security reminder
blocks.body: Template literals are not automatically safe for DOM or SQL. Use parameterized queries, DOMPurify, or framework escaping. Tagged templates are the extension point for domain-specific safety.

interviewTakeaways: Backticks allow multi-line strings and ${expression} interpolation.
Tagged templates call fn(strings, ...values) — strings include static parts only.
String.raw preserves escape sequences in raw segments.
60s: JS `${x}` equals C# $"{x}". Tags power CSS-in-JS and sanitizers. Never trust user input in HTML templates.
Follow-up: how would you implement a tag that escapes HTML entities?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'Template literals auto-escape HTML' — they do not; coercion is plain ToString.
Weak: 'Tags only return strings' — tags can return React elements or AST nodes.
Strong: 'Use tags for DSL safety. String.raw for regex paths. Treat ${userInput} in HTML like any XSS vector.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# $"{name}" maps to `Hello ${name}`. C# raw triple-quoted strings map to backtick multi-line literals. C# has no tagged template equivalent — use FormattableString for culture-safe formatting.
TypeScript adds template literal types (`on${Event}`) at compile time — separate from run-time template literals. Both share backtick syntax in different phases.
